questions.stem:
Trace this nested selection with `x = 5` and `y = 20`. What is the final value of `r`?

`if x > 10: { if y > 10: r = 1 else: r = 2 } else: { if y > 10: r = 3 else: r = 4 }`
questions.explanation: Evaluate the outer condition first: `x > 10` is `5 > 10`, which is false, so control enters the outer `else` branch. Inside it, `y > 10` is `20 > 10`, which is true, so `r = 3`. The inner tests in the discarded branch are never evaluated at all.

distractorRationale.a: Takes the `then` branch of both tests, ignoring that `x > 10` is false
distractorRationale.b: Evaluates the outer test correctly as false but then follows the inner `else`, ignoring that `y > 10` is true
distractorRationale.d: Follows the `else` branch at both levels, treating `y > 10` as false

questions.stem: A program must read lines from a file until it reaches a sentinel line reading `END`. Which iteration construct is appropriate, and why?

options.text: A counting `for` loop, because file reading is always definite iteration
A `while` loop, because the number of iterations is not known before the loop begins
A `for` loop over the integers 1 to 1000, because files are bounded in size
Recursion, because loops cannot test a condition on data read inside the body

questions.explanation: This is **indefinite iteration**: the trip count depends on data discovered during execution, so it cannot be computed in advance. A condition-controlled `while` loop is the correct construct. A counting `for` loop expresses **definite iteration**, where the trip count is fixed before the first iteration.

distractorRationale.a: Iterating a file line by line is definite only when the line count is known beforehand, which it is not here
distractorRationale.c: An arbitrary upper bound is a guess; it either truncates a long file or performs useless iterations
distractorRationale.d: Recursion would work but is not required — a `while` loop tests its condition on data read in the previous iteration perfectly well

questions.stem:
How many times does the statement `count = count + 1` execute?

`for i = 1 to n:`
`    for j = i to n:`
`        count = count + 1`
questions.explanation: The inner loop starts at $j = i$, not at 1, so for a given $i$ it executes $n - i + 1$ times. Summing over $i = 1, \dots, n$ gives $n + (n-1) + \dots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Note that this is still $\Theta(n^2)$ — halving the constant does not change the growth class.

distractorRationale.a: Assumes the inner loop always runs $n$ times, which would be correct only if it started at $j = 1$
distractorRationale.c: Off by one: this counts $n - i$ iterations per pass, forgetting that $j = i$ itself is executed
distractorRationale.d: Adds the two loop bounds instead of summing the nested trip counts

questions.stem: For a positive integer `n`, how many times does the body of `for (i = 0; i <= n; i = i + 1)` execute?
questions.explanation: The counter takes every integer value from 0 to $n$ inclusive, and the number of integers in the closed interval $[0, n]$ is $n + 1$. This is the classic fence-post error: the half-open form `i < n` runs $n$ times, whereas the closed form `i <= n` runs one extra time and will index one past the end of an $n$-element array.

distractorRationale.a: Counts the interval as open at both ends
distractorRationale.b: Applies the trip count of the half-open idiom `i < n` to a closed condition

options.text: A variable whose value never changes anywhere inside the loop body
A condition that holds before the first iteration and is preserved by every iteration
The condition that causes the loop to terminate
The number of iterations the loop will perform

questions.explanation: An invariant is an assertion true at the loop's entry point on every pass. Proving a loop correct requires three parts: **initialisation** (the invariant holds before the first iteration), **maintenance** (if it holds at the start of an iteration it holds at the start of the next), and **termination** (when the loop exits, the invariant plus the negated guard imply the desired postcondition).

distractorRationale.a: Confuses an invariant with a loop constant. A useful invariant almost always mentions variables that do change, such as "`sum` equals the total of the first `i` elements"
distractorRationale.c: That is the negation of the loop guard, which is used alongside the invariant at termination, not in place of it
distractorRationale.d: That is the trip count or a loop variant, used to prove termination rather than partial correctness

questions.stem: In a language with short-circuit `&&`, the guard `if (i < n && a[i] == target)` is safe when `i` equals `n`, but `if (a[i] == target && i < n)` is not.
questions.explanation: True. Short-circuit `&&` evaluates its right operand only if the left operand is true. In the first form, `i < n` is false when `i == n`, so `a[i]` is never evaluated and the out-of-bounds access cannot occur. In the second form the index expression is evaluated first, so it reads `a[n]` before the bound is ever tested. Ordering a short-circuit conjunction so the guard precedes the guarded expression is a correctness requirement, not a style preference.

questions.stem: The loop `while (n > 1) { n = floor(n / 2); k = k + 1 }` starts with `n = 1000` and `k = 0`. What is the final value of `k`? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: The sequence of values `n` takes is 1000, 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1, so the body executes nine times. In general a halving loop from $n$ performs $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ iterations, and $\lfloor \log_2 1000 \rfloor = 9$ because $2^9 = 512 \le 1000 < 1024 = 2^{10}$. This is why halving loops are $O(\log n)$.

questions.stem:
What is the final value of `total`?

`total = 0`
`for i = 1 to 6:`
`    if i mod 2 == 0: continue`
`    if i > 4: break`
`    total = total + i`
questions.explanation: `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and advances the counter; `break` exits the loop entirely. So $i = 1$ adds 1 (total 1); $i = 2$ is even and is skipped; $i = 3$ adds 3 (total 4); $i = 4$ is skipped; $i = 5$ is odd but $5 > 4$, so the loop breaks before the addition. The final total is 4.

distractorRationale.b: Sums the even values 2 and 4, inverting the `mod 2 == 0` test
distractorRationale.c: Sums 1, 3 and 5, treating `break` as `continue` and adding 5 before exiting
distractorRationale.d: Sums every value from 1 to 6, ignoring both `continue` and `break`
